trial_name: CRASH-2 — Effects of Tranexamic Acid on Death, Vascular Occlusive Events, and Blood Transfusion in Trauma Patients (2010)
citation: CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage (CRASH-2): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9734):23-32.
trial_type: RCT — international, double-blind, placebo-controlled, pragmatic, superiority
one_liner: Early administration of tranexamic acid reduces all-cause mortality and death due to bleeding in adult trauma patients with or at risk for significant hemorrhage without increasing vascular occlusive events.

pico.population: Adult trauma patients presenting within 8 hours of injury with significant hemorrhage (e.g., SBP < 90 mmHg, HR > 110 bpm) or at risk of significant hemorrhage.
pico.intervention: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading dose infused over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV maintenance infusion over 8 hours.
pico.comparison: Matched placebo (identical infusion schedule) plus usual trauma care.
pico.outcome: 28-day all-cause mortality, bleeding death, vascular occlusive events, and blood product transfusion requirements.

background.existing_knowledge: Among trauma patients who reach the hospital alive, hemorrhage is a leading preventable cause of early mortality.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether early short-course antifibrinolytic therapy safely reduces fatal bleeding without increasing thromboembolic complications in trauma.
background.hypothesis: Early administration of tranexamic acid reduces death (overall and from bleeding) without increasing vascular occlusive events in adult trauma patients with or at risk of significant hemorrhage.

methods.design: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, pragmatic, international multicentre trial across 274 hospitals in 40 countries.
methods.setting: 274 hospitals across 40 countries; enrollment within 8 hours of injury.

inclusion: Adult trauma patients within 8 hours of injury
Significant hemorrhage (e.g., SBP < 90 mmHg and/or HR > 110 bpm) or considered at risk of significant hemorrhage based on clinician judgment
exclusion: Enrolment > 8 hours after injury (recorded as protocol deviation in 23 patients)
Age < 16 years (recorded as protocol deviation in 5 patients)
Non-traumatic hemorrhage (recorded as protocol deviation in 9 patients)

methods.intervention: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading dose over 10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV maintenance infusion over 8 hours (mean time since injury at randomisation ~2.8 hours).
methods.comparison: Matched placebo infusion (10-minute loading + 8-hour infusion) plus usual trauma care (transfusion, surgery, hemostatic adjuncts).
methods.blinding: Double-blind (patients, treating clinicians, and trial personnel masked); sequential numbered treatment packs; emergency unblinding not required.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 20,000 patients to detect a relative risk of 0.90 for all-cause mortality assuming 20% baseline mortality (85% power at P < 0.01 and 95% power at P < 0.05).
methods.primary_outcome: All-cause mortality within 4 weeks (in-hospital follow-up up to 28 days).
secondary_outcomes: Vascular occlusive events (MI, stroke, PE, DVT; fatal or non-fatal)
Dependency/functional status at discharge or day 28
methods.follow_up: In-hospital follow-up to death, discharge, or 28 days.

headline_bullets: TXA significantly reduced all-cause mortality (14.5% vs 16.0%, RR 0.91) and death due to bleeding (4.9% vs 5.7%, RR 0.85).
Vascular occlusive events were not significantly increased with TXA (1.7% vs 2.0%, RR 0.84).
Blood product transfusion rates and surgical intervention rates were virtually identical between groups.

outcomes_table.note: Cause-specific death classification as recorded by sites
Fatal or non-fatal MI, stroke, PE, or DVT
Includes neurosurgery, chest, abdominal, or pelvic surgery
Functional status assessed at discharge or day 28
Full recovery at discharge or day 28

safety: Any vascular occlusive event (MI, stroke, PE, DVT): 168/10060 (1.7%) vs 201/10067 (2.0%), RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.68–1.02, P=0.084)

domains.notes: Centralized sequence generation with allocation via sequentially numbered packs (20,116 allocations) and telephone randomisation (95 allocations); strict concealment.
Double-blind trial using identical matched placebo infusions; emergency unblinding was not required.
Intention-to-treat analysis; only 4 patients removed post-randomisation due to consent withdrawal.
Fixed dosing schedule; minor protocol deviations included 23 enrolled >8h, 5 aged <16, and 9 with non-traumatic bleeding.
Prognostic baseline variables closely matched (mean age 34.6 vs 34.5 years, male 83.6% vs 84.0%, blunt trauma 67.5% vs 67.7%, mean time since injury 2.8 vs 2.9 hours).

internal_validity.verdict: High overall internal validity for the primary objective mortality endpoint, with residual uncertainty concentrated in clinician-diagnosed secondary safety endpoints.

domains.notes: Massive international cohort across 274 hospitals in 40 countries using pragmatic inclusion criteria.
Broadly applicable to adult trauma with suspected bleeding, though variation in trauma system maturity and VTE screening practices exists across international sites.

external_validity.verdict: High external validity for early TXA administration in adult trauma patients with suspected significant bleeding.

strengths: Extremely large sample size (20,211 randomized patients across 40 countries)
Double-blind placebo-controlled design with complete allocation concealment
Near-complete follow-up for the primary endpoint
Low-cost, highly accessible, and easily scalable therapeutic intervention
limitations: Secondary safety events relied on clinical diagnosis, risking under-ascertainment of non-fatal VTE
Transfusion volume and surgical intervention rates were pragmatic, crude proxies for bleeding control
Lack of granular post-randomization protocol adherence details regarding maintenance infusion completion

critical_appraisal.summary: Landmark international pragmatic RCT providing high-certainty evidence that early TXA administration safely reduces mortality in bleeding trauma patients.
strengths: Pragmatic design reflecting real-world clinical decision-making
Minimal lost-to-follow-up in a global setting
weaknesses: Inability to detect exact mechanisms due to crude transfusion tracking
Pragmatic variability in diagnostic testing for thromboembolic events

sections.authors_conclusion: Tranexamic acid safely reduces all-cause mortality and death due to bleeding in trauma patients with or at risk of significant hemorrhage.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Administer TXA (1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours) as early as possible to adult trauma patients with or at risk for significant hemorrhage.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult trauma patients presenting within 3 hours of injury with physiological signs of shock (e.g., SBP < 90 mmHg, HR > 110 bpm) or clinician-assessed risk of major bleeding.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean TXA should be initiated > 3 hours after injury, nor does it replace surgical source control or balanced blood transfusion.
implementation_caveats: Time-critical therapy: maximum efficacy requires administration as early as possible (< 1–3 hours from injury)
Administration > 3 hours post-injury is associated with potential harm/increased bleeding death
Total blood product requirements may not show a measurable reduction despite improved survival

controversies.notes: Mortality was significantly reduced despite no detectable overall difference in blood product transfusions or surgical intervention rates.

Subsequent exploratory analysis showed bleeding mortality reduction was greatest when TXA was given ≤1 hour (RR 0.68; 95% CI 0.57–0.82) and 1–3 hours (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.64–0.97), while treatment >3 hours increased mortality due to bleeding (RR 1.44; 95% CI 1.12–1.84).
Reliance on clinical diagnosis without routine protocolized screening in a pragmatic trial raised concerns for potential VTE under-reporting.
Viscoelastic testing data suggest potential harm if TXA is given to patients in a physiological fibrinolytic shutdown state.

context_related_trials.relation: Prehospital RCT evaluating early prehospital TXA dosing schemes in trauma.
Prehospital RCT evaluating bolus plus infusion TXA strategy on functional outcomes in severe trauma.

unresolved_questions: Role of viscoelastic assays (TEG/ROTEM) to tailor TXA administration to hyperfibrinolytic phenotypes
Optimal prehospital dosing strategies and candidates in mature trauma networks

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Give TXA (1 g IV over 10 min + 1 g IV over 8 h) as early as possible and within 3 hours to trauma patients with significant bleeding to reduce mortality.
